questions.stem: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}$ is classified as
questions.explanation: Amines are classified by the number of hydrogen atoms of ammonia replaced by alkyl or aryl groups. In dimethylamine two hydrogens are replaced by two methyl groups, leaving one N-H bond, so it is a secondary amine. The groups are alkyl, so it is aliphatic.

optionRationale.2: A primary amine has only one alkyl group on nitrogen.
optionRationale.3: A tertiary amine has three alkyl groups and no N-H bond.
optionRationale.4: There is no aromatic ring in this compound.

questions.objective: Classify an amine

questions.stem: The IUPAC name of $\mathrm{CH_3NHCH_2CH_3}$ is
questions.explanation: In IUPAC naming of secondary amines the longest alkyl chain on nitrogen gives the parent name. Here it is the ethyl group, so the parent is ethanamine. The other group, methyl, is shown on nitrogen using N-, giving N-methylethanamine.

optionRationale.1: The longer chain is the parent, so ethanamine is the parent and methyl is the substituent.
optionRationale.2: This is not an IUPAC name; the substituent on nitrogen is shown with the prefix N-.
optionRationale.4: This is a primary amine isomer with an unbranched three-carbon chain.

questions.objective: Name a secondary amine by IUPAC rules

questions.stem: Ethylamine is treated with $\mathrm{NaNO_2}$ and dilute HCl at 273 K. The main organic product is
questions.explanation: Nitrous acid generated from NaNO$_2$ and HCl converts a primary aliphatic amine into an unstable aliphatic diazonium salt. This decomposes at once, losing nitrogen gas, to give a carbocation which reacts with water to form the alcohol, with some other products.

optionRationale.1: Nitrile formation would need an alkyl halide and cyanide.
optionRationale.2: Aliphatic diazonium salts are unstable and decompose immediately.
optionRationale.3: Nitroethane is made from AgNO2 and bromoethane, not from the amine.

questions.objective: Predict the reaction of a primary aliphatic amine with nitrous acid

questions.stem: Ethanamide is reduced with lithium aluminium hydride. The product is
questions.explanation: Amides are reduced by LiAlH$_4$ so that the carbonyl group C=O is converted into CH$_2$ while the nitrogen stays attached. Thus CH$_3$CONH$_2$ becomes CH$_3$CH$_2$NH$_2$, an amine with the same number of carbon atoms.

optionRationale.1: The C-N bond is not cleaved; the carbonyl is reduced to CH2 rather than to alcohol.
optionRationale.3: This has one carbon less and would be the Hofmann bromamide product.
optionRationale.4: This needs dehydration of the amide, not reduction.

questions.objective: Recall reduction of amides to amines

questions.stem: Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol in a mildly alkaline medium to give
questions.explanation: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile and attacks the activated para position of the phenoxide ion. The product has an N=N link between the rings, and is called an azo compound, here p-hydroxyazobenzene. Such azo compounds are coloured and used as dyes.

optionRationale.2: No nitro group is introduced because the reagent contains the diazonium group.
optionRationale.3: Chlorobenzene would need CuCl, not phenol.
optionRationale.4: This needs two phenyl groups joined through oxygen, which does not occur here.

questions.objective: Recall the coupling reaction of diazonium salts

questions.stem: Ethylamine reacts with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine to give
questions.explanation: Primary and secondary amines are acylated by acid chlorides in nucleophilic substitution, with the amino hydrogen replaced by the acyl group. A base such as pyridine removes the HCl formed and shifts the equilibrium. Ethylamine gives N-ethylethanamide.

optionRationale.1: An ester would need ethanol and acetyl chloride.
optionRationale.2: This forms only by reaction with HCl, but here acylation takes place.
optionRationale.4: Only one ethyl group is on nitrogen as the amine had only one.

questions.objective: Predict the product of acylation of an amine

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT give the carbylamine (isocyanide) test with chloroform and alcoholic KOH?
questions.explanation: The carbylamine reaction is given only by primary amines, aliphatic or aromatic, because the NH$_2$ group loses both hydrogens to form the isocyanide R-N=C. Dimethylamine is a secondary amine and cannot lose two hydrogens in this way, so it gives no test.

optionRationale.1: Aniline is a primary amine, so it gives the foul-smelling phenyl isocyanide.
optionRationale.3: Methylamine is a primary amine and gives methyl isocyanide.
optionRationale.4: Ethylamine is a primary amine and gives the carbylamine test.

questions.objective: Identify compounds giving the carbylamine test

questions.stem: The pK$_b$ of ethylamine in water at 298 K is 3.25. What is the pK$_a$ of the ethylammonium ion at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: For a base and its conjugate acid, $pK_a + pK_b = pK_w = 14$ at 298 K. So $pK_a = 14 - 3.25 = 10.75$. A large pK$_a$ for the conjugate acid shows that ethylamine is a fairly strong base.

optionRationale.1: This repeats the pKb value instead of converting it.
optionRationale.2: This assumes neutral pH, which is not the relation between pKa and pKb.
optionRationale.3: This adds 14 to the pKb rather than subtracting.

questions.objective: Relate pKb of a base and pKa of its conjugate acid

questions.stem: Which of these amines has the highest $K_b$ value in water at a given temperature?
questions.explanation: In aqueous solution basicity depends on the +I effect, the solvation of the ammonium ion by hydrogen bonding, and steric factors. For methyl-substituted amines the order is (CH$_3$)$_2$NH > CH$_3$NH$_2$ > (CH$_3$)$_3$N > NH$_3$. The tertiary amine falls because its ion is poorly solvated.

optionRationale.1: Ammonia has no electron-releasing methyl group and is the weakest of the four.
optionRationale.2: This is a strong base, but weaker than the dimethyl compound in water.
optionRationale.4: Its basicity is lowered in water by poor solvation of the ion and steric hindrance.

questions.objective: Compare the basic strength of methylamines

questions.stem: Benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with hypophosphorous acid ($\mathrm{H_3PO_2}$) and water. The main product is
questions.explanation: Hypophosphorous acid acts as a reducing agent and replaces the diazonium group by hydrogen, liberating nitrogen. The product is benzene. This is used to remove an amino group after it has served to direct other substituents on the ring.

optionRationale.2: Phenol forms when the diazonium salt is warmed with water alone.
optionRationale.3: Chlorobenzene needs CuCl/HCl in the Sandmeyer reaction.
optionRationale.4: Iodobenzene is formed with KI, not with a reducing acid.

questions.objective: Recall replacement of the diazonium group by hydrogen

questions.stem: 6.05 g of benzamide (molar mass 121 g mol$^{-1}$) is subjected to Hofmann bromamide degradation with 80 % yield. What mass of aniline (molar mass 93 g mol$^{-1}$) is obtained?
questions.explanation: Moles of benzamide = 6.05/121 = 0.05 mol. The reaction converts one mole of the amide into one mole of the amine, so the theoretical mass of aniline is 0.05 x 93 = 4.65 g. With 80 % yield, mass = 4.65 x 0.80 = 3.72 g.

optionRationale.1: This is the theoretical yield without the 80 % factor.
optionRationale.2: This uses the molar mass of benzamide instead of aniline.
optionRationale.3: This divides by the yield instead of multiplying.

questions.objective: Calculate the yield of a Hofmann bromamide reaction

questions.stem: 1.18 g of a primary aliphatic amine $\mathrm{RNH_2}$ is exactly neutralised by 20.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl. The amine is
questions.explanation: A primary amine reacts with HCl in 1:1 ratio. Moles of HCl = 1.00 x 0.0200 = 0.0200 mol, so moles of amine = 0.0200. Molar mass = 1.18/0.0200 = 59 g mol$^{-1}$. The molar mass of C$_3$H$_7$NH$_2$ is 36 + 7 + 14 + 2 = 59, which fits.

optionRationale.1: Its molar mass is 31 g per mole, much lower than the calculated 59.
optionRationale.3: Its molar mass is 45 g per mole, which does not match the data.
optionRationale.4: Its molar mass is 73 g per mole, which is higher than the calculated value.

questions.objective: Find an amine from a titration with acid

questions.stem: How many secondary amines are possible for the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}$?
questions.explanation: Secondary amines carry two alkyl groups on nitrogen with a total of four carbons: methyl with n-propyl, methyl with isopropyl, and ethyl with ethyl. That gives N-methylpropan-1-amine, N-methylpropan-2-amine and N-ethylethanamine, a total of 3.

optionRationale.1: This misses one of the three combinations of two alkyl groups with a total of four carbons.
optionRationale.2: Four is the number of primary amine isomers, not of secondary amines.
optionRationale.4: N-ethylethanamine is only one of three secondary isomers.

questions.objective: Count structural isomers of secondary amines

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of basic strength of ethyl amines in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: In water, basicity is the balance of +I effect, solvation of the cation by hydrogen bonding, and steric hindrance. For ethylamines the secondary amine gets the best balance, and the tertiary amine is next because of reduced solvation. The order is (C$_2$H$_5$)$_2$NH > (C$_2$H$_5$)$_3$N > C$_2$H$_5$NH$_2$ > NH$_3$.

optionRationale.1: This is the order in the gas phase, where solvation does not matter.
optionRationale.2: This ignores the greater +I effect of two ethyl groups.
optionRationale.3: Ammonia is the weakest, since it lacks any electron-releasing alkyl group.

questions.objective: Predict the basicity order of ethylamines in water

questions.stem: Aniline is treated first with acetic anhydride, then with bromine in acetic acid, and the product is hydrolysed. The major final product is
questions.explanation: Aniline is so activated that bromine water gives the tribromo product. Acetylation to acetanilide reduces the electron-donating power of nitrogen because its lone pair also delocalises into the carbonyl group. Bromination then gives mainly the para product, and hydrolysis restores the amino group to give p-bromoaniline.

optionRationale.2: This forms directly from aniline and bromine water, but the acetylation lowers the activation.
optionRationale.3: The acetamido group is ortho and para directing, so no major meta product.
optionRationale.4: Bromination occurs on the ring, not at the nitrogen, under these conditions.

questions.objective: Use protection by acetylation to control substitution

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.010 M solution of a weak amine with $K_b = 1.0\times10^{-6}$ at 298 K? (Neglect the change in the amine concentration.)
questions.explanation: For a weak base, $[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_b C} = \sqrt{1.0\times10^{-6} \times 0.010} = 1.0\times10^{-4}$ M. Then pOH = 4.0 and pH = 14 - 4.0 = 10.0. The assumption that the ionised fraction is small holds because $1.0\times10^{-4}$ is only 1 % of 0.010.

optionRationale.1: This is the pOH of the solution, not the pH.
optionRationale.3: This results from taking [OH-] = Kb, not applying the square root relation.
optionRationale.4: This results from [OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-3, which would need a Kb of 1.0 x 10^-4.

questions.objective: Calculate the pH of a weak base solution

questions.stem: Trimethylamine reacts with nitrous acid to form
questions.explanation: A tertiary amine has no N-H bond to lose, so with nitrous acid it only accepts a proton to form a trialkylammonium nitrite salt, which dissolves in water. Primary aliphatic amines liberate nitrogen to give alcohols, and secondary amines give yellow oily N-nitrosoamines.

optionRationale.1: This is the product of a secondary amine, not a tertiary amine.
optionRationale.2: This is the result with a primary aliphatic amine.
optionRationale.4: Only primary aromatic amines form stable diazonium salts at low temperature.

questions.objective: Compare the reactions of primary, secondary and tertiary amines with HNO2

questions.stem: The sulphonamide formed from a primary amine and benzenesulphonyl chloride dissolves in aqueous KOH because
options: the N-H hydrogen is made acidic by the sulphonyl group
the sulphonamide forms a hydrogen bond with all alkali
it contains a free carboxyl group
the alkali hydrolyses it to the free amine
questions.explanation: In RNH-SO$_2$C$_6$H$_5$, the hydrogen on nitrogen is attached to an atom linked to a strongly electron-withdrawing sulphonyl group, so it is acidic. Alkali removes it and forms a water-soluble sodium salt. A secondary amine's sulphonamide has no such hydrogen, so it stays insoluble.

optionRationale.2: Hydrogen bonding alone does not make the compound dissolve as a salt.
optionRationale.3: No carboxyl group is present in the sulphonamide.
optionRationale.4: Under the test conditions the sulphonamide is not hydrolysed; it only forms a salt.

questions.objective: Explain the Hinsberg test

questions.stem: Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with aniline in a weakly acidic medium to give
questions.explanation: The diazonium ion couples as an electrophile with the para position of aniline, which is activated by the amino group. The product retains the -N=N- linkage between two rings, and is p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow azo dye. The medium is weakly acidic to keep aniline free.

optionRationale.1: No nitro group is introduced, because the reagent has only the diazonium nitrogen.
optionRationale.3: This needs the loss of the diazonium nitrogen, but here the N=N link is retained.
optionRationale.4: This is the reduction product of azobenzene, not the coupling product.

questions.objective: Recall coupling with aromatic amines

questions.stem: Which of the following primary amines of formula $\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}$ is chiral?
questions.explanation: A chiral carbon needs four different groups. In butan-2-amine, CH$_3$CH(NH$_2$)CH$_2$CH$_3$, carbon 2 carries H, NH$_2$, CH$_3$ and C$_2$H$_5$, all different, so the molecule is chiral. The other three primary isomers have no carbon with four different substituents.

optionRationale.1: The carbon bearing nitrogen is a CH2 with two identical hydrogens, so not chiral.
optionRationale.2: The carbon bearing nitrogen has three identical methyl groups.
optionRationale.3: No carbon in this chain has four different groups.

questions.objective: Identify a chiral amine

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia in aqueous solution.
Reason (R): The methyl group releases electrons by the +I effect and increases the electron density on nitrogen.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The methyl group pushes electron density towards nitrogen, which makes the lone pair more available for accepting a proton. The methylammonium ion is also stabilised. Both statements are true and the reason correctly explains the greater basicity.

optionRationale.2: The +I effect directly explains the greater availability of the lone pair, so R explains A.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true; alkyl groups release electrons by the +I effect.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true; methylamine is more basic than ammonia.

questions.objective: Explain basicity with the inductive effect

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Ethylamine has a much higher boiling point than propane, though their molar masses are almost equal.
Reason (R): Ethylamine is a polar molecule.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Ethylamine can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds through its N-H groups, whereas propane is non-polar and held only by weak dispersion forces. Ethylamine is indeed polar, but the main cause of the higher boiling point is hydrogen bonding, which R does not name. Both are true with R not the best explanation.

optionRationale.1: Polarity alone does not explain it, since the hydrogen bonding is the key factor.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true; ethylamine has a polar N-H bond and a lone pair.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true; amines boil much higher than alkanes of similar mass.

questions.objective: Account for the boiling points of amines

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Gabriel phthalimide synthesis gives pure primary amines free from secondary and tertiary amines.
Reason (R): Gabriel synthesis is suitable for preparing aromatic primary amines from aryl halides.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The phthalimide anion can be alkylated only once, so hydrolysis releases a primary amine only, which is why the products are pure. The aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion, so aromatic amines cannot be made this way. Thus A is true and R is false.

optionRationale.1: The reason is false: aryl halides do not react in Gabriel synthesis.
optionRationale.2: The reason is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: only primary amines are formed.

questions.objective: Recall the scope of Gabriel synthesis

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Aniline is a stronger base than ethylamine.
Reason (R): In aniline the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Delocalisation of the lone pair into the ring makes it less available for protonation, so aniline is a weaker base than ethylamine, where the alkyl group increases electron density. The assertion is false, but the reason is a true statement about aniline.

optionRationale.1: The assertion is false, since aniline is the weaker base.
optionRationale.2: The assertion is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true; the lone pair participates in resonance with the ring.

questions.objective: Compare the basicity of aromatic and aliphatic amines

questions.stem: Match the amine in List-I with its class in List-II.
questions.explanation: Ethylamine has one alkyl group and is a primary aliphatic amine (A-III). Dimethylamine has two methyl groups and is a secondary aliphatic amine (B-IV). Trimethylamine has three and is a tertiary aliphatic amine (C-I). Aniline has one phenyl group, so it is a primary aromatic amine (D-II).

optionRationale.1: This swaps the matches of C and D: C is actually I and D is actually II.
optionRationale.3: This swaps the matches of A and D: A is actually III and D is actually II.
optionRationale.4: This swaps the matches of B and C: B is actually IV and C is actually I.

questions.objective: Match amines with their classification

questions.stem: Match the conversion in List-I with the reagent in List-II.
questions.explanation: Nitriles are reduced to primary amines with LiAlH$_4$ (A-II). Nitrobenzene is reduced to aniline with tin and HCl (B-I). Ethanamide gives methylamine, with one carbon less, by the Hofmann bromamide reaction using Br$_2$ and NaOH (C-IV). Pure primary amines from alkyl halides come from Gabriel synthesis (D-III).

optionRationale.2: This swaps the matches of B and D: B is actually I and D is actually III.
optionRationale.3: This swaps the matches of C and D: C is actually IV and D is actually III.
optionRationale.4: This swaps the matches of A and C: A is actually II and C is actually IV.

questions.objective: Match conversions with reagents

left: D. Alkyl halide to a pure primary amine
right: III. Potassium phthalimide, then alkaline hydrolysis

questions.stem: Match the test in List-I with the observation in List-II.
questions.explanation: The sulphonamide of a primary amine has an acidic N-H and dissolves in alkali (A-IV). That of a secondary amine has no N-H, so it stays insoluble (B-II). Diazotisation followed by coupling with 2-naphthol gives an orange-red azo dye (C-III). Primary amines give foul-smelling isocyanides in the carbylamine test (D-I).

optionRationale.1: This swaps the matches of A and D: A is actually IV and D is actually I.
optionRationale.2: This swaps the matches of A and C: A is actually IV and C is actually III.
optionRationale.4: This swaps the matches of A and B: A is actually IV and B is actually II.

questions.objective: Match the tests for amines with the observations

left: A. Primary amine with benzenesulphonyl chloride, then alkali
B. Secondary amine with benzenesulphonyl chloride, then alkali
C. Aromatic primary amine with NaNO$_2$/HCl at 273 K, then alkaline 2-naphthol
D. Primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic KOH
right: II. Product remains insoluble in alkali

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about amines.
A. Primary and secondary amines form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
B. Tertiary amines do not form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other.
C. Among isomeric amines the boiling point order is primary > secondary > tertiary.
D. Amines have higher boiling points than alcohols of comparable molar mass.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: N-H bonds in primary and secondary amines allow intermolecular hydrogen bonding, whereas tertiary amines have no N-H (A and B true). Therefore among isomers the boiling points fall from primary to tertiary (C true). Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so alcohols form stronger hydrogen bonds and boil higher (D false).

optionRationale.1: D is false; alcohols boil higher than amines because O-H hydrogen bonds are stronger than N-H.
optionRationale.2: D is false, and A and C are also correct.
optionRationale.3: D is false and B and C are also correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on physical properties of amines

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about diazonium salts.
A. The diazonium group can be replaced by -CN using CuCN.
B. Benzenediazonium chloride can be stored indefinitely in solution at room temperature.
C. Aromatic diazonium salts are more stable than aliphatic ones because of resonance with the ring.
D. Benzenediazonium fluoroborate is stable at room temperature and insoluble in water.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: CuCN replaces the diazonium group by cyanide in the Sandmeyer reaction (A true). The solution is stable only at 273-278 K and decomposes on standing at room temperature (B false). Resonance with the ring stabilises aromatic diazonium ions (C true). The fluoroborate salt is stable and insoluble in water (D true).

optionRationale.1: Statement B is false; the solution decomposes on standing above 278 K.
optionRationale.2: B is false, and A and C are also correct.
optionRationale.3: This omits statement D, which is also correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on diazonium salts

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about aniline.
A. Aniline darkens on exposure to air and light.
B. In the nitrating mixture, aniline is protonated, and the anilinium ion directs the nitro group to the meta position.
C. Aniline undergoes the Friedel-Crafts reaction readily.
D. Acetylation of the amino group reduces its activating influence on the ring.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Freshly distilled aniline is colourless but turns brown on exposure to air through oxidation (A true). In strongly acidic nitrating mixtures the anilinium ion forms and directs meta (B true). The amino group reacts with AlCl$_3$ to form a salt, which blocks Friedel-Crafts reactions (C false). Acetylation delocalises the lone pair into the carbonyl group, moderating the activation (D true).

optionRationale.2: Statement C is false; aniline forms a salt with AlCl3, so Friedel-Crafts reactions fail.
optionRationale.3: C is false and A is also correct.
optionRationale.4: This omits statement B, which is also correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the reactions of aniline
